Glossary\n75\t\n76\tSeveral of these words are overloaded in the surrounding literature, and two of them\n77\t(*block*, *frame*) mean different things in different research documents. Within this\n78\tplan they mean exactly this:\n79\t\n80\t| Term | Meaning here |\n81\t|---|---|\n82\t| **Fragment** | The atomic unit the fountain code operates over. Fixed length **L** for the whole session (D15). |\n83\t| **K** | Number of fragments in one block. Derived as `blockSize / L`; never transmitted (D7). |\n84\t| **Block** | A contiguous slice of the (possibly compressed) payload, cut into K fragments and fountain-coded independently. **Always means this** — never \"fountain block\" or \"QR block\". |\n85\t| **Packet** | One fountain-coded symbol: 13-byte header + L payload bytes. The unit a tile carries. |\n86\t| **Tile** | One QR symbol on screen. Carries exactly one packet. |\n87\t| **Frame** | One displayed image, containing a grid of tiles. **Never** a video frame — those are *camera frames*. |\n88\t| **Camera frame** | One image captured by the receiver's camera. |\n89\t| **Beacon** | A special **packet** carrying file-level metadata instead of payload. Beacon packets are encoded into tiles and mixed into display frames by the frame mixer (D17, §7.2). |\n90\t| **Profile** | A modulation configuration: QR version, module pixel size, tile count. Several coexist per frame (D16). |\n91\t| **Dwell** | How many packets the sender emits for one block before advancing (§8.1). |\n92\t| **Screen px** | A pixel on the *sender's display*. What the renderer controls. |\n93\t| **Camera px** | A pixel in the *receiver's captured frame*. What the decoder actually sees. |\n94\t| **px/module** | **Always CAMERA px per module unless explicitly written \"screen px/module\".** The 4 px/module decode cliff is a *camera*-pixel figure. Conflating the two put every S2/S3 optical run below the cliff — see `../notes/spike-results.md` §S3. |\n95\t| **Magnification** | `camera_px_per_module = screen_px_per_module × M`, where `M` = (capture width across the code region) / (code region width in screen px). A 1920-px-wide landscape code region filling a 1080-px-wide portrait capture gives **M = 0.5625**, so 4 screen px/module is only **2.25 camera px/module**. |\n96\t| **Erasure** | A packet that did not arrive or failed validation. Never a corrupted packet — those are discarded, not used. |\n97\t| **Stage** | A modulation generation: 1 = tiled mono QR, 2 = + RGB tripling, 3 = custom grid codec. |\n98\t| **Pass** | One complete traversal of every block by the sender. |\n99\t\n100\t---\n101\t\n102\t## 3. What multi-gigabyte breaks, and the fix\n103\t\n104\tFour assumptions in the pre-multi-GB design do not survive contact with a 4 GB file.\n105\t\n106\t### 3.1 The fountain decoder does not scale — in TIME, not memory\n107\t\n108\tThis is the correction the plan review surfaced, and it matters because the first\n109\tversion of this section got it half right.\n110\t\n111\tD5 chose an LT code with a **Gaussian elimination** decoder, verified at\n112\t[`sim/`](../research/sim/). GE costs O(K²) in *memory* and O(K³) in *bit operations*.\n113\tThe original block-layer decision sized K from the memory term alone and concluded 4 MB\n114\tblocks (K = 16,384) were fine because the coefficient matrix is only 32 MB.\n115\t\n116\t**The memory term was never the binding constraint. Time is.**\n117\t\n118\tEach arriving packet is reduced against up to `rank` stored pivot rows; each row\n119\toperation XORs the coefficient mask (K/8 bytes) *and* the payload (L bytes). Reaching\n120\tfull rank costs `W = 2 · (K²/2) · (K/8 + L) = K² · (K/8 + L)` bytes of memory traffic,\n121\tand the block only lasts `K·L / R` seconds at wire rate R — so the decoder must\n122\t**sustain**:\n123\t\n124\t```\n125\trequired = W / (K·L/R) = K · (K/8 + L) · R / L    bytes/sec\n126\t```\n127\t\n128\t> The leading factor is **1, not 2** — the 2 and the /2 in `W` cancel. A previous\n129\t> revision of this section printed `2 · K · (K/8 + L) · R / L` and was 2× too\n130\t> pessimistic in every derived figure. Gate **G7** now diffs this section against the\n131\t> model so the class of error cannot recur.\n132\t\n133\tAll figures below are emitted by\n134\t[`sim/ge_cost_model.py`](../research/sim/ge_cost_model.py) — this section quotes the\n135\tmodel rather than reasoning beside it. **All rows at Stage 1 (R = 30 KB/s)**, so they\n136\tare comparable:\n137\t\n138\t| K | L | Block | Matrix | Work/block | Sustained need | |\n139\t|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n140\t| 1,000 | 1260 | 1.2 MB | 122.1 KB | 1.3 GB | 33.8 MB/s | research baseline |\n141\t| 1,500 | 1260 | 1.8 MB | 274.7 KB | 3.0 GB | 52.9 MB/s | research partitioning ceiling |\n142\t| 4,000 | 1260 | 4.8 MB | 1.9 MB | 26.2 GB | 171.6 MB/s | research called this **\"too slow\"** |\n143\t| **16,384** | **256** | **4.0 MB** | **32.0 MB** | **576.0 GB** | **4.5 GB/s** | **23× over budget** |\n144\t\n145\tThe plan's own evidence base\n146\t([`fountain-codes-and-protocol.md`](../research/fountain-codes-and-protocol.md) §2.6)\n147\tstates: *\"Cost scales as K², so it must be bounded. At K = 4000 the decode work is ~16×\n148\tthat of K = 1000 (~6 GB of XOR) — too slow\"* and recommends *\"source-block partitioning\n149\tabove K ≈ 1500\"*. **K = 16,384 was 11× past that ceiling.**\n150\t\n151\tIt was worse than a simple overshoot: shrinking L to 256 B to fit small tiles made the\n152\tmask term (K/8 = 2048 B) dominate the payload term (256 B) by 8×, so the decode problem\n153\tgot *harder* as a side effect of a decision made for a different reason.\n154\t\n155\t**Two further findings from the model:**\n156\t\n157\t- **A faster wire rate makes decode harder** — same work, less time to do it. So K MUST\n158\t  be sized for the *fastest* stage we intend to reach (Stage 3, 106 KB/s), not the\n159\t  slowest. This is counterintuitive and is why the original error was easy to make.\n160\t- **The sender's cost was unbudgeted too.** §6.3.1 counted QR encode and render but not\n161\t  the fountain XOR. At uncapped harmonic degree and K = 16,384 that is 398 KB of XOR\n162\t  per packet — **91.8 MB/s** at the old 225 packets/s (1 packet/tile), or **183.6 MB/s**\n163\t  at the adopted 450 packets/s (2 packets/tile at R2 nominal), on top of everything\n164\t  else. Hence D25.\n165\t\n166\t**Fix — D19:** K = **768**, L = **256 B**, block = **192.0 KB**.\n167\t\n168\t| | Was | Now |\n169\t|---|---|---|\n170\t| K | 16,384 | **768** |\n171\t| L | 256 B | **256 B** (unchanged — see §3.1.1) |\n172\t| Block | 4 MB | **192.0 KB** |\n173\t| GE matrix | 32.0 MB | **72.0 KB** |\n174\t| Block-layer working set | ~36 MB (claimed) | **264.0 KB** |\n175\t| Sustained need @ Stage 3 | 14.9 GB/s | **114.6 MB/s** |\n176\t\n177\t*Both \"sustained need\" figures are at Stage 3, so they compare like with like. The\n178\t4.5 GB/s in the table above is the same design at Stage 1.*\n179\t\n180\t**K_max at Stage 3 is 1152.** We adopt **768** deliberately below the ceiling —\n181\tD26 requires the sender to assume the weaker receiver, and the 200 MB/s budget is\n182\titself an unmeasured estimate (§18 R1). Margin at Stage 3: **1.74×**.\n183\t\n184\t| K | Block | Stage 1 | Stage 2 | Stage 3 | |\n185\t|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n186\t| 512 | 128.0 KB | 19.7 MB/s | 39.3 MB/s | 69.5 MB/s | 2.88× margin |\n187\t| **768** | **192.0 KB** | **32.4 MB/s** | **64.9 MB/s** | **114.6 MB/s** | **adopted, 1.74× margin** |\n188\t| 1024 | 256.0 KB | 47.2 MB/s | 94.4 MB/s | 166.7 MB/s | 1.20× margin |\n189\t| 1152 | 288.0 KB | 55.3 MB/s | 110.6 MB/s | 195.4 MB/s | 1.02× — the ceiling |\n190\t| 1536 | 384.0 KB | 82.6 MB/s | 165.2 MB/s | 291.8 MB/s | 1.5× **over** at Stage 3 |\n191\t\n192\t### 3.1.1 L is set by the *conservative* ladder rung, not the nominal one\n193\t\n194\tA revision of this plan briefly set L = 507 B (\"one packet per v15 tile\") and broke\n195\tD16's ladder. What multi-gigabyte breaks, and the fix\n\nFour assumptions in the pre-multi-GB design do not survive contact with a 4 GB file.\n\n### 3.1 The fountain decoder does not scale — in TIME, not memory\n\nThis is the correction the plan review surfaced, and it matters because the first\nversion of this section got it half right.\n\nD5 chose an LT code with a **Gaussian elimination** decoder, verified at\n[`sim/`](../research/sim/). GE costs O(K²) in *memory* and O(K³) in *bit operations*.\nThe original block-layer decision sized K from the memory term alone and concluded 4 MB\nblocks (K = 16,384) were fine because the coefficient matrix is only 32 MB.\n\n**The memory term was never the binding constraint. Time is.**\n\nEach arriving packet is reduced against up to `rank` stored pivot rows; each row\noperation XORs the coefficient mask (K/8 bytes) *and* the payload (L bytes). Reaching\nfull rank costs `W = 2 · (K²/2) · (K/8 + L) = K² · (K/8 + L)` bytes of memory traffic,\nand the block only lasts `K·L / R` seconds at wire rate R — so the decoder must\n**sustain**:\n\n```\nrequired = W / (K·L/R) = K · (K/8 + L) · R / L    bytes/sec\n```\n\n> The leading factor is **1, not 2** — the 2 and the /2 in `W` cancel. A previous\n> revision of this section printed `2 · K · (K/8 + L) · R / L` and was 2× too\n> pessimistic in every derived figure. Gate **G7** now diffs this section against the\n> model so the class of error cannot recur.\n\nAll figures below are emitted by\n[`sim/ge_cost_model.py`](../research/sim/ge_cost_model.py) — this section quotes the\nmodel rather than reasoning beside it. **All rows at Stage 1 (R = 30 KB/s)**, so they\nare comparable:\n\n| K | L | Block | Matrix | Work/block | Sustained need | |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| 1,000 | 1260 | 1.2 MB | 122.1 KB | 1.3 GB | 33.8 MB/s | research baseline |\n| 1,500 | 1260 | 1.8 MB | 274.7 KB | 3.0 GB | 52.9 MB/s | research partitioning ceiling |\n| 4,000 | 1260 | 4.8 MB | 1.9 MB | 26.2 GB | 171.6 MB/s | research called this **\"too slow\"** |\n| **16,384** | **256** | **4.0 MB** | **32.0 MB** | **576.0 GB** | **4.5 GB/s** | **23× over budget** |\n\nThe plan's own evidence base\n([`fountain-codes-and-protocol.md`](../research/fountain-codes-and-protocol.md) §2.6)\nstates: *\"Cost scales as K², so it must be bounded. At K = 4000 the decode work is ~16×\nthat of K = 1000 (~6 GB of XOR) — too slow\"* and recommends *\"source-block partitioning\nabove K ≈ 1500\"*. **K = 16,384 was 11× past that ceiling.**\n\nIt was worse than a simple overshoot: shrinking L to 256 B to fit small tiles made the\nmask term (K/8 = 2048 B) dominate the payload term (256 B) by 8×, so the decode problem\ngot *harder* as a side effect of a decision made for a different reason.\n\n**Two further findings from the model:**\n\n- **A faster wire rate makes decode harder** — same work, less time to do it. So K MUST\n  be sized for the *fastest* stage we intend to reach (Stage 3, 106 KB/s), not the\n  slowest. This is counterintuitive and is why the original error was easy to make.\n- **The sender's cost was unbudgeted too.** §6.3.1 counted QR encode and render but not\n  the fountain XOR. At uncapped harmonic degree and K = 16,384 that is 398 KB of XOR\n  per packet — **91.8 MB/s** at the old 225 packets/s (1 packet/tile), or **183.6 MB/s**\n  at the adopted 450 packets/s (2 packets/tile at R2 nominal), on top of everything\n  else. Hence D25.\n\n**Fix — D19:** K = **768**, L = **256 B**, block = **192.0 KB**.\n\n| | Was | Now |\n|---|---|---|\n| K | 16,384 | **768** |\n| L | 256 B | **256 B** (unchanged — see §3.1.1) |\n| Block | 4 MB | **192.0 KB** |\n| GE matrix | 32.0 MB | **72.0 KB** |\n| Block-layer working set | ~36 MB (claimed) | **264.0 KB** |\n| Sustained need @ Stage 3 | 14.9 GB/s | **114.6 MB/s** |\n\n*Both \"sustained need\" figures are at Stage 3, so they compare like with like. The\n4.5 GB/s in the table above is the same design at Stage 1.*\n\n**K_max at Stage 3 is 1152.** We adopt **768** deliberately below the ceiling —\nD26 requires the sender to assume the weaker receiver, and the 200 MB/s budget is\nitself an unmeasured estimate (§18 R1). Margin at Stage 3: **1.74×**.\n\n| K | Block | Stage 1 | Stage 2 | Stage 3 | |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| 512 | 128.0 KB | 19.7 MB/s | 39.3 MB/s | 69.5 MB/s | 2.88× margin |\n| **768** | **192.0 KB** | **32.4 MB/s** | **64.9 MB/s** | **114.6 MB/s** | **adopted, 1.74× margin** |\n| 1024 | 256.0 KB | 47.2 MB/s | 94.4 MB/s | 166.7 MB/s | 1.20× margin |\n| 1152 | 288.0 KB | 55.3 MB/s | 110.6 MB/s | 195.4 MB/s | 1.02× — the ceiling |\n| 1536 | 384.0 KB | 82.6 MB/s | 165.2 MB/s | 291.8 MB/s | 1.5× **over** at Stage 3 |\n\n### 3.1.1 L is set by the *conservative* ladder rung, not the nominal one\n\nA revision of this plan briefly set L = 507 B (\"one packet per v15 tile\") and broke\nD16's ladder. D15's source note states the governing rule plainly: **pick L to fit the\nsmallest tile any profile would use.** At L = 507 the packet is 520 B and the\nconservative rung, v10-L, holds **271 B** — so it could carry **zero** packets, only\nbeacons. That destroys the ladder's one load-bearing property: *a mis-guessed profile\nyields zero; a ladder always yields something.*\n","numLines":200,"startLine":1,"totalLines":1567}}}

{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"call_079ff20e4e604996be762af8","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t# Fountain Codes and Wire Protocol for screenferry\n2\t\n3\tResearch notes for the erasure-coding and framing layer of **screenferry** — a static web app\n4\tthat moves a file device-to-device over a strictly one-way optical channel (sender shows\n5\tanimated QR codes, receiver's camera decodes them).\n6\t\n7\tChannel properties that drive every decision below:\n8\t\n9\t- **No back-channel.** The receiver cannot NAK, cannot request a chunk, cannot say \"stop\".\n10\t- **Lossy and bursty.** Focus hunting, motion blur, glare, the user pointing the phone away,\n11\t  and plain decoder misses. Realistic per-frame loss `p` is 0.1–0.5 depending on how steady\n12\t  the hands are and how aggressive the frame rate is.\n13\t- **Receiver may join at any time.** There is no \"frame 1\"; the receiver starts when the\n14\t  camera opens.\n15\t\n16\tAll simulation numbers in this document were produced locally (Monte Carlo, 60–2000 trials\n17\tper cell); the scripts are reproducible from the descriptions given inline.\n18\t\n19\t---\n20\t\n21\t## 1. The coupon-collector penalty\n22\t\n23\t### 1.1 Formula\n24\t\n25\tBroadcast `N` chunks round-robin forever. Frame `f` carries chunk `f mod N`. Each frame is\n26\tindependently lost with probability `p`.\n27\t\n28\tThink in **rounds** of `N` frames. A specific chunk is still missing after `k` rounds with\n29\tprobability `p^k` (it was offered `k` times, missed every time). The number of rounds `R`\n30\tuntil *all* `N` chunks have been seen at least once satisfies\n31\t\n32\t```\n33\tP(R ≤ k) = (1 − p^k)^N\n34\t```\n35\t\n36\tso the expected number of rounds is\n37\t\n38\t```\n39\t              ∞\n40\tE[R]  =  Σ   [ 1 − (1 − p^k)^N ]\n41\t            k=0\n42\t```\n43\t\n44\tand the expected number of **frames displayed** is `≈ N · E[R]` (slightly less, because the\n45\tfinal round terminates part-way through).\n46\t\n47\tThe closed-form asymptotic is the classic coupon-collector `ln N` law, rescaled by how many\n48\trounds it takes for one chunk to get through:\n49\t\n50\t```\n51\tE[R]  ≈  ( ln N + γ ) / ln(1/p)  +  1/2          (γ ≈ 0.5772)\n52\t```\n53\t\n54\tThe `ln N` term is the whole problem: **the cost per chunk grows with the file size**, even\n55\tthough the channel's loss rate is constant. A fountain code removes the `ln N` entirely.\n56\t\n57\t### 1.2 Worked numbers\n58\t\n59\t`E[frames]` and `p95` below are exact Monte Carlo (2000 trials for N ≤ 500, 200 for\n60\tN = 5000). \"Fountain\" is `N × 1.05 / (1 − p)` — a rateless code needing 5 % overhead.\n61\t\n62\t| N | p | E[rounds] | **E[frames]** | p95 frames | Fountain frames | **Penalty** |\n63\t|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|\n64\t| 50 | 0.1 | 2.44 | 108 | 156 | 58 | **1.85×** |\n65\t| 50 | 0.3 | 4.24 | 192 | 290 | 75 | **2.56×** |\n66\t| 50 | 0.5 | 6.99 | 332 | 509 | 105 | **3.16×** |\n67\t| 500 | 0.1 | 3.44 | 1 563 | 2 004 | 583 | **2.68×** |\n68\t| 500 | 0.3 | 6.14 | 2 870 | 3 866 | 750 | **3.83×** |\n69\t| 500 | 0.5 | 10.30 | 4 925 | 6 691 | 1 050 | **4.69×** |\n70\t| 5000 | 0.1 | 4.44 | 20 440 | 24 789 | 5 833 | **3.50×** |\n71\t| 5000 | 0.3 | 8.05 | 38 556 | 51 973 | 7 500 | **5.14×** |\n72\t| 5000 | 0.5 | 13.62 | 65 804 | 85 702 | 10 500 | **6.27×** |\n73\t\n74\t### 1.3 Reading these numbers in wall-clock terms\n75\t\n76\tTake a **630 KB file** at 1 260 payload bytes per frame → `N = 500`, displayed at **8 fps**,\n77\twith a middling `p = 0.3`:\n78\t\n79\t| Scheme | Frames | Wall clock | 95th percentile |\n80\t|---|---:|---:|---:|\n81\t| Round-robin | 2 870 | **6 min 00 s** | **8 min 03 s** |\n82\t| Fountain (5 % overhead) | 750 | **1 min 34 s** | ~1 min 40 s |\n83\t\n84\tThe mean is bad; the **tail is worse and it is the tail users experience**. Round-robin's\n85\tp95/mean ratio is ~1.35 and grows with `p`, because finishing means waiting for the single\n86\tunluckiest chunk to come round again. A fountain code has an almost deterministic completion\n87\ttime — its p99 overhead is within a few percent of its mean (measured: 1.04–1.11× at\n88\tN ≥ 100, see §2.5). That predictability is arguably worth more than the raw speedup: the\n89\tprogress bar moves smoothly and monotonically instead of hanging at 99 %.\n90\t\n91\t**Three structural wins, not one:**\n92\t\n93\t1. **No `ln N` term.** Fountain cost is `N(1+ε)/(1−p)` — linear in N, flat in N per chunk.\n94\t   Round-robin cost per chunk grows without bound as the file grows.\n95\t2. **Loss-rate agnostic.** Round-robin's penalty *multiplies* as `p` rises; a rateless code\n96\t   just runs `1/(1−p)` longer. No parameter has to be guessed in advance — which matters\n97\t   enormously when there is no back-channel to measure `p` with.\n98\t3. **Free join-anywhere.** With round-robin the receiver must be told (or infer) where the\n99\t   loop starts. With a fountain code every frame is equally useful, so \"point the camera at\n100\t   it\" is the entire user interface.\n101\t\n102\t---\n103\t\n104\t## 2. Fountain / rateless code candidates\n105\t\n106\t### 2.0 Terms\n107\t\n108\t- **K** — number of source fragments (chunks) the payload is split into.\n109\t- **Overhead ε** — receiver decodes after `K(1+ε)` *received* symbols. Frames *sent* is\n110\t  `K(1+ε)/(1−p)`.\n111\t- **Peeling / belief-propagation decoder** — repeatedly find a received symbol of degree 1,\n112\t  use it to recover a fragment, XOR that fragment out of every other symbol. O(K·d̄). Cheap\n113\t  but stalls whenever no degree-1 symbol exists.\n114\t- **Inactivation / Gaussian-elimination decoder** — treat received symbols as rows of a\n115\t  linear system over GF(2) and solve it. Never stalls; decodes as soon as rank = K. Costs\n116\t  more arithmetic.\n117\t\n118\tThe single most important finding of this research is that **the choice of decoder matters\n119\tmore than the choice of degree distribution**, and that the decoder everybody's LT\n120\timplementation ships (peeling) is the wrong one for screenferry's small `K`.\n121\t\n122\t### 2.1 LT codes (Luby, 2002) with robust soliton\n123\t\n124\tEncode: pick a degree `d` from a distribution, pick `d` distinct source fragments uniformly,\n125\tXOR them. Repeat forever. Decode: peeling.\n126\t\n127\tThe **ideal soliton** distribution is `ρ(1) = 1/K`, `ρ(d) = 1/(d(d−1))` for `d ≥ 2`. It has\n128\t*expected* behaviour that is perfect and *actual* behaviour that is terrible — it produces\n129\texactly one degree-1 symbol in expectation, so the peeling ripple dies constantly. The\n130\t**robust soliton** adds a spike `τ` around `K/R` with `R = c·ln(K/δ)·√K` to keep the ripple\n131\talive; overhead is `O(√K · ln²(K/δ))` symbols, i.e. `ε → 0` only asymptotically.\n132\t\n133\tMeasured (peeling decoder, 400 trials/cell, `c = 0.03`, `δ = 0.5`):\n134\t\n135\t| K | ideal soliton mean ε | ideal p99 | robust soliton mean ε | robust p99 |\n136\t|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|\n137\t| 10 | **+71 %** | +370 % | **+62 %** | +280 % |\n138\t| 20 | **+77 %** | +370 % | **+57 %** | +205 % |\n139\t| 50 | **+67 %** | +402 % | **+44 %** | +194 % |\n140\t| 100 | **+69 %** | +337 % | **+33 %** | +116 % |\n141\t| 200 | **+65 %** | +321 % | **+26 %** | +105 % |\n142\t| 500 | **+65 %** | +273 % | **+19 %** | +50 % |\n143\t| 1000 | **+53 %** | +272 % | **+11 %** | +21 % |\n144\t\n145\t**This is the \"LT codes are poor for small N\" result, quantified.** At K = 50 — a 63 KB file\n146\tat 1.26 KB/frame, an utterly typical screenferry transfer — robust-soliton LT with a peeling\n147\tdecoder needs **44 % more symbols than the file contains, on average**, and one run in a\n148\thundred needs **nearly 3×**. Robust soliton only becomes respectable around K ≥ 1000, which\n149\tfor screenferry means a 1.3 MB file — the *upper* end of what anyone will sit through.\n150\t\n151\tThe `p99` column is the damning one. A 4× tail means \"sometimes the transfer just doesn't\n152\tfinish and the user gives up\". screenferry cannot afford that.\n153\t\n154\t**Verdict on textbook LT: do not ship it as specified.** Keep the *encoder* (it is trivial),\n155\tthrow away the *decoder*.\n156\t\n157\t### 2.2 Raptor / RaptorQ (RFC 6330)\n158\t\n159\tRaptor codes fix LT's overhead by pre-coding: apply a high-rate fixed erasure code (LDPC +\n160\tHDPC) to the source block first, then run a *weakened* LT code over the pre-coded symbols.\n161\tThe pre-code mops up the fragments the LT layer fails to peel, so LT no longer has to reach\n162\t100 % on its own.\n163\t\n164\tRaptorQ (RFC 6330) is the standardised, systematic, GF(256)-mixed version. Its recovery\n165\tguarantee is exceptional and is stated directly in the reference implementation's README\n166\t([cberner/raptorq](https://github.com/cberner/raptorq)):\n167\t\n168\t> Reconstruction probability after receiving K + h packets = 1 − 1/256^(h + 1)\n169\t\n170\tThat is: **K symbols → 99.6 % decode. K+1 → 99.998 %. K+2 → 99.99999 %.** Overhead is\n171\teffectively `ε ≈ 0`. Nothing else in this document comes close. Decode is O(K) amortised\n172\twith inactivation decoding.\n173\t\n174\t**Costs:**\n175\t\n176\t- **Implementation difficulty in pure JS: very high.** RFC 6330 is ~60 pages of tables,\n177\t  including a hard-coded systematic-index table `J(K')`, 477 permitted block sizes `K'`,\n178\t  GF(256) arithmetic, and an LDPC/HDPC pre-code. Nobody should hand-write this. It is\n179\t  realistically a *wrap the Rust crate* proposition, not a *write it ourselves* one.\n180\t- **Licensing: improved but not perfectly clean.** Qualcomm (which acquired Digital Fountain\n181\t  in 2009) filed an IPR declaration for RFC 6330 with the IETF on 2015-03-19\n182\t  ([IPR #2554](https://datatracker.ietf.org/ipr/2554/)) listing US7,139,960; US7,451,377;\n183\t  US20090158114; EP1665539; US20110299629. The declaration is **not** a blanket royalty-free\n184\t  grant — it is two-tier:\n185\t  - *Wireless WAN devices*: licensed under Qualcomm's standard terms, no incremental royalty.\n186\t  - *Non-wireless devices*: **covenant not to assert** — \"Qualcomm will not assert any such\n187\t    claim against any party for making, using, selling, importing or offering for sale such\n188\t    device\" — limited to RFC 6330 implementation, with a defensive-termination carve-out.\n189\t\n190\t  Separately, the foundational patent **US7,139,960 is now listed as expired**\n191\t  ([Google Patents](https://patents.google.com/patent/US7139960)), and the continuation\n192\t  US20110299629 (filed 2011) runs to ~2031. So: the core Raptor idea is out of patent, the\n193\t  RaptorQ-specific continuations are not, and there is a covenant covering exactly our use\n194\t  case. **Risk is low but non-zero**, and it is the kind of footnote that makes a\n195\t  general-audience open-source project awkward to explain.\n196\t- **Bundle cost:** see §3 — 240 KB of WASM (134 KB gzipped).\n197\t\n198\t**Verdict: technically the best code, wrong cost/benefit for screenferry.** We are paying 134 KB\n199\tof gzipped WASM plus a patent footnote to buy back ~2–3 % of overhead versus the scheme\n200\trecommended in §7. On a 500-frame transfer that is ~15 frames — under two seconds.\n201\t\n202\t### 2.3 Online codes (Maymounkov, 2002)\n203\t\n204\tTwo-layer like Raptor, but both layers are simple XOR and both are rateless-friendly. An\n205\t*outer* encoding attaches each message block to ~`0.55·q·ε·n` auxiliary blocks (each\n206\tauxiliary block = XOR of its attached message blocks); an *inner* encoding emits check blocks\n207\twhose degree comes from a distribution parameterised by `ε` and `F`. With suggested\n208\tparameters `q = 3`, `ε = 0.01`, the message decodes from `(1 + 3ε)n` check blocks with\n209\tfailure probability `(ε/2)^(q+1)`\n210\t([Wikipedia: Online codes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Online_codes)).\n211\t\n212\t**Assessment for screenferry:** Online codes are *nicer to implement than Raptor and no harder\n213\tthan LT*, and they are unencumbered (Maymounkov published academically; no assignee ever\n214\tpursued the classic Raptor claims against them). But:\n215\t\n216\t- The `(1+3ε)n` guarantee is **asymptotic in n**. The auxiliary-block layer costs `0.55qεn`\n217\t  extra blocks up front — at `ε = 0.01, q = 3` that is 1.65 % of n, but the *constants* in\n218\t  the failure analysis only bite for large n. At K = 50–500 you are back in the same\n219\t  small-block regime that hurts LT, and the parameters need retuning per K with no published\n220\t  small-K tables.\n221\t- There is **no maintained JS implementation** to lean on.\n222\t- Its main advantage over a GE decoder — O(K) rather than O(K²)-ish decode — is irrelevant at\n223\t  our K.\n224\t\n225\t**Verdict: no reason to prefer it over §7's scheme.** Strictly more moving parts (two layers,\n226\ttwo parameter sets) for no measurable win at our block sizes.\n227\t\n228\t### 2.4 XOR interleaving and block-wise Reed–Solomon\n229\t\n230\tThe low-complexity alternative: forget rateless codes, pick a fixed rate.\n231\t\n232\t**Reed–Solomon over GF(256)** is *MDS* — RS(n, k) recovers from **exactly** k received\n233\tsymbols out of n, which is information-theoretically optimal (ε = 0 *exactly*, better than\n234\tRaptorQ's probabilistic guarantee). Implementations are small (log/antilog tables, ~200 lines)\n235\tand well understood.\n236\t\n237\tIt is nonetheless **the wrong tool here, for one decisive reason: it is not rateless.**\n238\t\n239\t- GF(256) caps a codeword at `n ≤ 255` symbols. To tolerate `p = 0.5` you need `n ≥ 2k`, so\n240\t  `k ≤ 127` per block. Files larger than ~160 KB need interleaved blocks, and now a bad burst\n241\t  that lands on one block kills the transfer while the others sit fully decoded.\n242\t- **You must commit to a rate before transmitting, with no back-channel to inform the\n243\t  choice.** Guess `p = 0.3` and hit `p = 0.6` and the transfer *never completes* — the sender\n244\t  runs out of repair symbols and the receiver stalls forever. Guess `p = 0.6` and hit\n245\t  `p = 0.1` and you waste 50 % of the airtime. There is no recovery from a wrong guess except\n246\t  restarting the whole transfer with different parameters, which is exactly the failure mode\n247\t  screenferry exists to eliminate.\n248\t- Simple **XOR interleaving** (parity every k-th frame, RAID-5 style) is worse still: it\n249\t  survives one loss per group and nothing more. Bursty camera loss routinely kills two\n250\t  adjacent frames.\n251\t\n252\t**Verdict: reject.** Ratelessness is not a nice-to-have on a channel with no feedback; it is\n253\tthe entire requirement. RS's optimal-ε is worthless if the rate is wrong, and the rate is\n254\talways wrong.\n255\t\n256\t### 2.5 The finding that changes the answer: swap the decoder\n257\t\n258\tEverything in §2.1 assumed a **peeling** decoder, because that is what LT means in practice\n259\tand what every LT library ships. But at screenferry's block sizes we can afford to just *solve the\n260\tlinear system* — the received symbols are rows over GF(2), and Gaussian elimination decodes\n261\tthe instant the matrix reaches rank K, which is the information-theoretic optimum for that\n262\tmatrix.\n263\t\n264\tSame simulation, same degree distributions, **full GF(2) Gaussian elimination** instead of\n265\tpeeling. \"harmonic\" is `Pr(d) ∝ 1/d`, the distribution BC-UR uses (§4.4):\n266\t\n267\t| K | dist | peeling mean ε | **GE mean ε** | **GE p99 ε** |\n268\t|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|\n269\t| 10 | ideal soliton | +71 % | **+26 %** | +120 % |\n270\t| 10 | harmonic | +56 % | **+30 %** | +140 % |\n271\t| 50 | robust soliton | +44 % | **+14 %** | +74 % |\n272\t| 50 | harmonic | +89 % | **+6.7 %** | +20 % |\n273\t| 100 | robust soliton | +33 % | **+6.6 %** | +30 % |\n274\t| 100 | harmonic | +108 % | **+3.9 %** | +10 % |\n275\t| 200 | harmonic | +127 % | **+2.5 %** | +6.5 % |\n276\t| 500 | harmonic | +156 % | **+1.5 %** | +3.0 % |\n277\t| 1000 | harmonic | +181 % | **+1.2 %** | +2.2 % |\n278\t\n279\tTwo things jump out:\n280\t\n281\t1. **Gaussian elimination is transformative.** At K = 100 the harmonic distribution goes from\n282\t   *+108 % overhead with peeling* to *+3.9 % with GE* — a 2× end-to-end speedup from changing\n283\t   nothing but the decoder. At K ≥ 200 the overhead is within a few percent of RaptorQ's,\n284\t   for ~80 lines of bit-twiddling and zero patent surface.\n285\t2. **The best distribution depends on the decoder, and they are opposites.** Robust soliton\n286\t   is *designed* for peeling and is mediocre under GE (it deliberately emits many degree-1\n287\t   symbols, which are linearly redundant). The harmonic distribution is *terrible* for\n288\t   peeling (and gets worse as K grows: +181 % at K = 1000) but is **excellent** under GE.\n289\t   Anyone benchmarking a fountain code must state which decoder they used; the rankings\n290\t   invert.\n291\t\n292\tThis reframes the entire decision. The question is no longer \"which fountain code\" — it is\n293\t\"**which degree distribution feeds a GE decoder best, and can we afford GE?**\"\n294\t\n295\t### 2.6 Can we afford Gaussian elimination? Bounding the cost\n296\t\n297\tGE over GF(2) with K unknowns is O(K³/w) word-operations on the coefficient matrix (`w = 32`\n298\twith `Uint32Array`), plus O(K²) XORs of `fragLen`-byte payloads. The **payload XORs dominate**.\n299\t\n300\tMeasured total row-XOR count (forward elimination + back-substitution), and the resulting\n301\taverage encoder degree:\n302\t\n303\t| K | distribution | mean ε | p99 ε | row-XORs / K | avg degree |\n304\t|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|\n305\t| 100 | harmonic (uncapped) | +4.2 % | +11 % | 38 | 19.3 |\n306\t| 100 | harmonic, **d ≤ 64** | +4.5 % | +11 % | 36 | 13.2 |\n307\t| 100 | harmonic, d ≤ 32 | +6.4 % | +23 % | 31 | 7.8 |\n308\t| 100 | harmonic, d ≤ 16 | +19 % | +75 % | 25 | 4.7 |\n309\t| 300 | harmonic (uncapped) | +2.1 % | +5.0 % | 120 | 47.7 |\n310\t| 300 | harmonic, **d ≤ 64** | +3.3 % | +6.3 % | 99 | 13.6 |\n311\t| 300 | harmonic, d ≤ 16 | +34 % | +132 % | 65 | 4.7 |\n312\t| 1000 | harmonic (uncapped) | +1.2 % | +1.9 % | 415 | 132.7 |\n313\t| 1000 | harmonic, **d ≤ 64** | +3.0 % | +4.1 % | 310 | 13.4 |\n314\t| 1000 | harmonic, d ≤ 32 | +8.1 % | +43 % | 254 | 7.9 |\n315\t| 1000 | uniform, d ≤ 32 | **+0.2 %** | **+0.5 %** | 398 | 16.4 |\n316\t\n317\tConcrete cost at the worst realistic case (**K = 1000**, i.e. a 1.26 MB file at 1 260 B\n318\tfragments, harmonic capped at d ≤ 64):\n319\t\n320\t- **Encoder, per frame:** 13.4 × 1 260 B ≈ **17 KB of XOR**. At 10 fps that is 170 KB/s.\n321\t  Nothing. (Uncapped it would be 133 × 1 260 = 167 KB/frame, 1.7 MB/s — still fine, but 10×\n322\t  more work on a sender that is often a phone. **This is the argument for the d ≤ 64 cap.**)\n323\t- **Decoder, total:** 310 × 1000 = 310 000 row-XORs × 1 260 B ≈ **390 MB of byte-XOR**, which\n324\t  as `Uint32Array` word ops is ~98 M operations — **a few hundred milliseconds spread across\n325\t  the entire multi-minute transfer**, not a single stall.\n326\t- **Decoder, per frame (worst case):** one arriving frame is reduced against at most `rank`\n327\t  pivot rows → ≤ 1000 × 1 260 B = 1.26 MB of XOR. At 10 fps, 12.6 MB/s worst case. Comfortably\n328\t  real-time in a Web Worker; typical cost is far lower.\n329\t- **Matrix memory:** K × ⌈K/32⌉ words = 1000 × 32 × 4 B = **128 KB**. Payloads are 1.26 MB.\n330\t  Trivial.\n331\t\n332\t**Cost scales as K², so it must be bounded.** At K = 4000 the decode work is ~16× that of\n333\tK = 1000 (~6 GB of XOR) — too slow. Mitigation, in preference order:\n334\t\n335\t1. **Raise `fragLen`** (bigger QR version) — K falls linearly, work falls quadratically.\n336\t2. **Compress** (§6) — same effect.\n337\t3. **Source-block partitioning** above K ≈ 1500: split into `B` blocks of ≤ 1500 fragments,\n338\t   fountain-code each independently, round-robin the block index across frames (the header\n339\t   in §7.2 reserves 4 bits for this). Decode work drops from O(K²) to O(K²/B). This is\n340\t   exactly what RFC 6330 does and for exactly this reason.\n341\t\n342\tWith `fragLen = 1260` and deflate, K ≈ 1500 corresponds to a ~1.9 MB file — which at\n343\trealistic optical throughput (§5.3) takes over four minutes to transmit anyway. **Single-block\n344\tGE covers every transfer a human will actually sit through**; partitioning is an escape hatch.\n345\t\n346\t---\n347\t\n348\t## 3. Existing implementations (JS / TS / WASM)\n349\t\n350\tAll figures below were obtained by downloading the published tarballs from the npm registry\n351\tand measuring, not from documentation.\n352\t\n353\t### 3.1 `raptorq` — npm 1.7.24 — **a real wasm-bindgen build of the Rust crate**\n354\t\n355\tThe Rust crate [cberner/raptorq](https://github.com/cberner/raptorq) (389 ★, Apache-2.0,\n356\tactively maintained — last push 2026-06) **publishes a WASM build to npm**, which the search\n357\tresults did not surface but the registry confirms.\n358\t\n359\t| Property | Value |\n360\t|---|---|\n361\t| Version / license | 1.7.24 (published 2023-06-20) / **Apache-2.0** |\n362\t| Contents | `raptorq_bg.wasm`, `raptorq.js`, `raptorq.d.ts` — nothing else |\n363\t| WASM size | **240 516 B raw / 134 387 B gzipped** |\n364\t| Dependencies | **none** |\n365\t| Browser-usable | **Yes** — wasm-bindgen with `init(module_or_path)` + `initSync()` |\n366\t\n367\tAPI (from the shipped `raptorq.d.ts`):\n368\t\n369\t```ts\n370\tEncoder.with_defaults(data: Uint8Array, maximum_transmission_unit: number): Encoder\n371\tencoder.encode(repair_packets_per_block: number): Uint8Array[]\n372\tDecoder.with_defaults(transfer_length: bigint, maximum_transmission_unit: number): Decoder\n373\tdecoder.decode(packet: Uint8Array): Uint8Array | undefined\n374\tEncodingPacket.deserialize(data) → .source_block_number() / .encoding_symbol_id() / .data()\n375\t```\n376\t\n377\t**Caveat that matters for screenferry:** `encode(repair_packets_per_block)` returns a **finite\n378\tarray** of packets — it is a batch API, not an infinite generator. Truly endless streaming\n379\trequires either generating a large batch up front and looping it (which reintroduces a\n380\tcoupon-collector effect, just a much weaker one) or patching the crate. Also, the npm build\n381\tlags the crate (npm 1.7.24 from 2023 vs. crate activity in 2026).\n382\t\n383\t### 3.2 `luby-transform` — npm 0.2.0 — from the **qifi-dev/qrs** project\n384\t\n385\tThis is the most directly relevant existing library: it was extracted from\n386\t[qifi-dev/qrs](https://github.com/qifi-dev/qrs) (1 621 ★, MIT, TypeScript), *a QR-code file\n387\tstreaming app* — i.e. someone has already built roughly screenferry and open-sourced the codec.\n388\t\n389\t| Property | Value |\n390\t|---|---|\n391\t| Version / license | 0.2.0 (2025-02-03) / **MIT** |\n392\t| Size | 11 366 B ESM, **2 977 B gzipped** — genuinely tiny |\n393\t| Dependencies | `pako` (adds ~45 KB gzipped — avoidable, see §6) |\n394\t| Browser-usable | Yes, pure ESM `Uint8Array` in / out |\n395\t\n396\tAPI: `createEncoder(data, sliceSize, compress=true)` → `encoder.fountain()` is an **infinite\n397\tgenerator** — exactly the right shape for animated QR. `createDecoder()` / `addBlock()` /\n398\t`getDecoded()`.\n399\t\n400\t**Three design flaws that rule it out as-is:**\n401\t\n402\t1. **Ideal soliton, not robust soliton.** From the shipped `dist/index.mjs`:\n403\t   ```js\n404\t   probabilities[0] = 1 / k;\n405\t   for (let d = 2; d <= k; d++) probabilities[d - 1] = 1 / (d * (d - 1));\n406\t   ```\n407\t   That is textbook ideal soliton — the distribution that is *known* to fail in practice\n408\t   (§2.1, +67 % mean / +400 % p99 at K = 50).\n409\t2. **It transmits the fragment indices explicitly, at 4 bytes each.**\n410\t   ```js\n411\t   const header = new Uint32Array([indices.length, ...indices, k, bytes, checksum]);\n412\t   ```\n413\t   Header size is `4 × (degree + 4)` bytes. With ideal soliton the mean degree is ~`ln K`;\n414\t   at K = 500 that is ~6, so ~40 header bytes per frame — and high-degree symbols cost far\n415\t   more. BC-UR's PRNG-derived index selection (§4.4) achieves the same thing in **zero**\n416\t   bytes. This is a 3–10 % airtime tax for nothing.\n417\t3. **The decoder is a subset-reduction peeler**, not GE — so it inherits the §2.5 penalty.\n418\t\n419\t**Verdict: excellent reference implementation to read, wrong on all three axes to depend on.**\n420\tIts `LtDecoder.propagateDecoded` subset-reduction logic is however a genuinely clever\n421\tpeeling+ variant and worth studying.\n422\t\n423\t### 3.3 `@ngraveio/bc-ur` — npm 1.1.13 — the BC-UR reference JS implementation\n424\t\n425\t| Property | Value |\n426\t|---|---|\n427\t| Version / license | 1.1.13 (2026-02-20) / **MIT** |\n428\t| Repo | [ngraveio/bc-ur](https://github.com/ngraveio/bc-ur) — TypeScript, actively maintained |\n429\t| Size | 176 KB `dist/` (64 KB of JS) + 7 runtime deps |\n430\t| Dependencies | `crc`, `jsbi`, `assert`, `sha.js`, `cbor-sync`, `bignumber.js`, `@keystonehq/alias-sampling` |\n431\t| Browser-usable | Yes, but the dep tree (`assert`, `Buffer`, `jsbi`, `bignumber.js`) is Node-flavoured and needs polyfills/bundler shims |\n432\t\n433\tThe dependency list is the problem: `bignumber.js` + `jsbi` + `sha.js` + `assert` for what is\n434\tfundamentally 200 lines of XOR is a poor trade for a static app whose selling point is that it\n435\tis a single self-contained page. Ships source in `src/` though, so the fountain layer\n436\t(`fountainUtils.ts`, `fountainEncoder.ts`, `fountainDecoder.ts`, `xoshiro.ts`) is easy to\n437\tlift. **Read it; don't depend on it.**\n438\t\n439\t### 3.4 `bbqr` — npm 1.2.0\n440\t\n441\t| Property | Value |\n442\t|---|---|\n443\t| Version | 1.2.0 (2025-04-10) |\n444\t| License | **No `license` field in `package.json`**; GitHub reports `NOASSERTION`. Needs legal review before use. |\n445\t| Size | 240 987 B ESM / 154 288 B IIFE — large, because `consts.d.ts` alone is 30 KB of QR capacity tables |\n446\t| Dependencies | none |\n447\t\n448\tAPI: `splitQRs(input, fileType, {encoding, minSplit, maxSplit, minVersion, maxVersion})` /\n449\t`joinQRs()`. **No fountain code** (§4.5). Its *QR-version-selection* logic — pick the smallest\n450\tversion that fits the split — is the genuinely reusable idea here.\n451\t\n452\t### 3.5 `wirehair` — C++ with a WASM port\n453\t\n454\t[catid/wirehair](https://github.com/catid/wirehair) (389 ★, **BSD-3-Clause**, pushed\n455\t2026-07-31) is an O(N) fountain code for large data — faster asymptotically than RaptorQ's\n456\tO(N log N)-ish behaviour and explicitly designed for big blocks. A WASM build exists at\n457\t[kig/wirehair-wasm](https://github.com/kig/wirehair-wasm), building `wirehair_core.mjs` via\n458\tEmscripten.\n459\t\n460\t**Not viable for screenferry:** the WASM port is **not published to npm** (`wirehair` is not a\n461\tregistered package), so it must be built from source with Emscripten in CI — a heavy toolchain\n462\tdependency for a static site. Wirehair is also optimised for N in the tens of thousands; at\n463\tK ≈ 100–1000 its advantage over plain GE evaporates while its complexity does not.\n464\t\n465\t### 3.6 `fountain-js`\n466\t\n467\t**Not a fountain code.** npm `fountain-js` is a parser for *Fountain*, the screenplay markup\n468\tlanguage. Named in the task brief; ruled out here so nobody re-checks it.\n469\t\n470\t### 3.7 Summary\n471\t\n472\t| Library | License | gzip size | Rateless stream | Decoder | Verdict |\n473\t|---|---|---:|---|---|---|\n474\t| `raptorq` (wasm) | Apache-2.0 | 134 KB | batch only | inactivation | Best code, worst bundle |\n475\t| `luby-transform` | MIT | **3 KB** | ✅ infinite gen | peeling | Read it, don't use it |\n476\t| `@ngraveio/bc-ur` | MIT | ~25 KB + 7 deps | ✅ infinite | subset-reduction | Read it, don't use it |\n477\t| `bbqr` | ⚠️ NOASSERTION | ~50 KB | ❌ no FEC | n/a | QR-version logic only |\n478\t| `wirehair-wasm` | BSD-3 | not published | ✅ | inactivation | Needs Emscripten in CI |\n479\t\n480\t**Nothing on this list is both small and correctly decoded.** That, plus §2.5, is the case\n481\tfor implementing it ourselves.\n482\t\n483\t---\n484\t\n485\t## 4. Prior art\n486\t\n487\t### 4.1 TXQR (divan) — the one with real measurements\n488\t\n489\t[divan/txqr](https://github.com/divan/txqr) (3 157 ★, MIT, Go) is the best-documented\n490\tanimated-QR transfer, with two blog posts of actual benchmark data. It uses\n491\t`google/gofountain` (LT codes).\n492\t\n493\t**Baseline, non-fountain** ([Animated QR data transfer with Gomobile and\n494\tGopherjs](https://divan.dev/posts/animatedqr/)) — 13 KB payload, swept 3–12 fps, 100–1000 B\n495\tchunks, all four ECC levels:\n496\t\n497\t- **Best case: 1.4 s ≈ 9 KB/s** at 11 fps / 850 B chunks / ECC Medium — but *unstable*,\n498\t  because a missed frame forces a full loop wait and often a timeout.\n499\t- **Optimal fps ≈ 6–7** (~150 ms/frame). Higher fps did *not* help; the phone camera and\n500\t  decoder, not the display, are the bottleneck.\n501\t- **Optimal chunk size ≈ 550–900 B.** Below that, per-frame header overhead dominates; at\n502\t  1000 B, \"almost guaranteed miss of frames and timeout\".\n503\t- **Optimal ECC = Low (7 %).** Counter-intuitive but consistent: lower ECC → smaller/sparser\n504\t  QR → faster and more reliable camera decode. **The QR code's own error correction is the\n505\t  wrong place to spend redundancy; spend it in the fountain layer instead.**\n506\t- **Realistic expectation: 1–2 KB/s**, not the 9 KB/s peak.\n507\t\n508\t**With fountain codes** ([Fountain codes and animated QR](https://divan.dev/posts/fountaincodes/)):\n509\t\n510\t- **Record: ~13 KB in 501 ms** at 12 fps with **1 850 B** per QR code.\n511\t- Optimal chunk size moved *up* to **1 800–2 000 B** (from 550–900 B). Once missed frames stop\n512\t  being catastrophic you can afford denser QR codes and a worse per-frame decode rate.\n513\t- Usable fps ceiling rose from ~7 to **15**.\n514\t- **\"The variance of the time needed to decode plummeted significantly as there were no\n515\t  'expect the whole loop iteration' part.\"** — independent confirmation of §1.3: the tail\n516\t  improvement is the real prize.\n517\t- Practical approach: generate `N × redundancyFactor` frames assuming ~20 % loss and loop\n518\t  them, trading strict ratelessness for API stability.\n519\t\n520\t*Caveat on secondary sources:* a search result attributed \"129+ KB/s, ~30× prior art\" to txqr.\n521\tThat number appears in an AI-generated aggregator blog and is **not** in divan's primary\n522\tposts, which state 501 ms for ~13 KB (≈ 26 KB/s peak, 1–2 KB/s typical). Use the primary\n523\tfigures.\n524\t\n525\t**Lessons for screenferry:** (a) 6–15 fps, not 30; (b) ECC Low; (c) fountain coding *raises* the\n526\toptimal chunk size, so tune density after the codec is in place, not before; (d) variance\n527\treduction is the headline benefit.\n528\t\n529\t### 4.2 BC-UR / Multipart UR (Blockchain Commons) — **the most relevant prior art**\n530\t\n531\tThe animated-QR standard used across the hardware-wallet industry (Keystone, NGRAVE, Foundation\n532\tPassport, Sparrow, Gordian). Specs:\n533\t\n534\t- [BCR-2020-005: Uniform Resources](https://github.com/BlockchainCommons/Research/blob/master/papers/bcr-2020-005-ur.md)\n535\t- [BCR-2024-001: Multipart UR (MUR) Implementation Guide](https://github.com/BlockchainCommons/Research/blob/master/papers/bcr-2024-001-multipart-ur.md)\n536\t- [Animated QRs — Developer Resources](https://developer.blockchaincommons.com/animated-qrs/)\n537\t\n538\t**Architecture.** Hybrid **fixed-rate prefix + rateless tail**. Parts are numbered from 1.\n539\tParts with `seqNum ≤ seqLen` are *pure* fragments (systematic); parts with `seqNum > seqLen`\n540\tare XOR mixes. So a clean single pass decodes with zero overhead and zero linear algebra, and\n541\tthe fountain tail is there to repair losses.\n542\t\n543\t**Part structure** (CDDL from BCR-2024-001):\n544\t\n545\t```\n546\tpart = [\n547\t    uint32 seqNum,\n548\t    uint   seqLen,\n549\t    uint   messageLen,\n550\t    uint32 checksum,\n551\t    bytes  data\n552\t]\n553\t```\n554\t\n555\tCBOR-encoded, then Bytewords-encoded, then wrapped as `ur:<type>/<seqNum>-<seqLen>/<fragment>`.\n556\t\n557\t**The key idea screenferry should steal — zero-byte index transmission.** From the shipped\n558\t`src/fountainUtils.ts` of `@ngraveio/bc-ur@1.1.13`:\n559\t\n560\t```ts\n561\texport const chooseFragments = (seqNum, seqLength, checksum) => {\n562\t  if (seqNum <= seqLength) {\n563\t    return [seqNum - 1];               // systematic prefix\n564\t  } else {\n565\t    const seed = Buffer.concat([intToBytes(seqNum), intToBytes(checksum)]);\n566\t    const rng = new Xoshiro(seed);     // Xoshiro256**, seeded SHA256(seqNum‖checksum)\n567\t    const degree = chooseDegree(seqLength, rng);\n568\t    const indexes = [...new Array(seqLength)].map((_, i) => i);\n569\t    return shuffle(indexes, rng).slice(0, degree);\n570\t  }\n571\t}\n572\t```\n573\t\n574\tBecause both sides derive the index set from `(seqNum, checksum)` alone, **the wire carries no\n575\tindex list**. Contrast `luby-transform`'s 4-bytes-per-index (§3.2). The `checksum` field is\n576\tbeautifully overloaded: it is simultaneously the **PRNG seed**, the **session discriminator**\n577\t(two different messages produce different mixes, so parts can't be cross-contaminated), and\n578\tthe **final integrity check**. screenferry should copy this trick verbatim.\n579\t\n580\t**Degree distribution** — plain harmonic, `Pr(d) ∝ 1/d`, sampled via Walker–Vose alias:\n581\t\n582\t```ts\n583\tconst degreeProbabilities = [...new Array(seqLenth)].map((_, i) => 1 / (i + 1));\n584\t```\n585\t\n586\t**Decoder** (`src/fountainDecoder.ts`): *subset reduction*, not full GE. A new mixed part is\n587\treduced by every stored simple part and every stored mixed part whose index set is a strict\n588\tsubset (`reducePartByPart`), and conversely every stored part is reduced by the new one. This\n589\tis stronger than pure peeling but weaker than Gaussian elimination.\n590\t\n591\t**Measured cost of that decoder choice.** Simulating BC-UR exactly (harmonic + systematic\n592\tprefix + subset reduction) against a GE decoder on the identical symbol stream, over a channel\n593\twith per-frame loss `p`:\n594\t\n595\t| K | p | BC-UR ε | BC-UR frames sent | GE ε (non-systematic) | GE frames sent | **GE speedup** |\n596\t|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|\n597\t| 50 | 0.1 | +16 % | 65 | +6.9 % | 59 | 1.09× |\n598\t| 50 | 0.5 | +38 % | 137 | +6.2 % | 106 | **1.29×** |\n599\t| 100 | 0.3 | +32 % | 189 | +4.0 % | 149 | **1.27×** |\n600\t| 100 | 0.5 | +54 % | 308 | +4.1 % | 208 | **1.48×** |\n601\t| 300 | 0.3 | +44 % | 618 | +2.1 % | 441 | **1.40×** |\n602\t| 300 | 0.5 | +73 % | 1 036 | +2.1 % | 617 | **1.68×** |\n603\t\n604\t(Round-robin for the same K=300, p=0.5 case: 2 699 frames. So BC-UR is 2.6× better than naive,\n605\tand GE is 4.4× better.)\n606\t\n607\t**Two independent findings here:**\n608\t\n609\t1. **BC-UR's decoder leaves 30–70 % on the table at high loss**, and the gap *widens* with\n610\t   both K and p — precisely the conditions a phone camera creates. Anyone implementing BC-UR\n611\t   can get a large speedup, wire-format-compatible, by swapping the decoder for GE.\n612\t2. **The systematic prefix is a net loss on a lossy channel.** Non-systematic GE beat\n613\t   systematic GE in every cell (e.g. K=100, p=0.5: +4.1 % vs +11.8 %). Reason: after a lossy\n614\t   first pass, the receiver is missing a specific `p·K`-dimensional subspace, and a low-degree\n615\t   tail symbol restricted to that subspace is the zero vector with probability ~`2^-d` — a\n616\t   degree-1 tail symbol is wasted half the time at p = 0.5. Non-systematic symbols carry\n617\t   information about the whole space from frame one. The systematic prefix only pays off when\n618\t   loss is near zero, which never happens with a handheld camera.\n619\t\n620\t**Verdict: BC-UR's *framing* is the right model (PRNG-derived indices, checksum-as-session-id,\n621\tharmonic degrees). Its *decoder* and its *systematic prefix* are both worth discarding.**\n622\t\n623\t### 4.3 BBQr (Coinkite) — the deliberate non-fountain design\n624\t\n625\t[bbqr.org](https://bbqr.org/BBQr.html) / [coinkite/BBQr](https://github.com/coinkite/BBQr).\n626\tThe competing Bitcoin animated-QR format, shipped on COLDCARD.\n627\t\n628\t**8-character ASCII header, `B$` + 6 fields**, chosen to sit in QR *alphanumeric* mode:\n629\t\n630\t| Chars | Field | Values |\n631\t|---|---|---|\n632\t| 1–2 | Magic | `B$` |\n633\t| 3 | Encoding | `H` = hex, `2` = Base32, `Z` = zlib+Base32 |\n634\t| 4 | File type | `P` PSBT, `T` txn, `J` JSON, `C` CBOR, `U` UTF-8, `B` binary, `X` executable |\n635\t| 5–6 | Total parts | base-36, `00`–`ZZ` (1–1295) |\n636\t| 7–8 | Part index | base-36, `00`–`ZZ` |\n637\t\n638\t- Zlib with `wbits=10`, level 9, **compressed as a whole before splitting**. Ratios 4–58 %\n639\t  depending on entropy; the encoder tries `Z` and falls back to `2` if compression didn't help\n640\t  — a nice runtime heuristic worth copying (§6).\n641\t- **No fountain code — all N parts must be scanned.** Order-independent, but the full\n642\t  coupon-collector penalty applies.\n643\t- **No protocol-level checksum**: \"QR error correction suffices.\"\n644\t- Max ~2.78 MB (hex) / ~3.47 MB (Base32).\n645\t\n646\t**BC-UR vs BBQr:**\n647\t\n648\t| | BC-UR | BBQr |\n649\t|---|---|---|\n650\t| Loss handling | LT fountain, rateless | none — rescan until complete |\n651\t| Header | CBOR, binary, ~10–15 B | 8 ASCII chars |\n652\t| Encoding | Bytewords (alphanumeric) | Base32 / hex (alphanumeric) |\n653\t| Compression | none in spec | zlib, with fallback |\n654\t| Integrity | CRC-32 whole message | none |\n655\t| Max size | unbounded | ~3.5 MB |\n656\t| Complexity | high | very low |\n657\t\n658\tBBQr's argument is that for a 2–5 part PSBT the fountain machinery is not worth it — and at\n659\tK = 3 they are right (§1: at N = 50 the penalty is only 1.85×; at N = 3 it is negligible).\n660\t**screenferry's regime is K = 50–1500, where the argument inverts completely.** BBQr's transferable\n661\tlessons are its compression-with-fallback heuristic and its QR-version auto-selection, not its\n662\tFEC stance.\n663\t\n664\t### 4.4 Optar and PaperBak\n665\t\n666\tPaper-oriented, but the coding lessons carry: both face a *one-way, no-retransmit* channel.\n667\t\n668\t- [Twibright Optar](http://ronja.twibright.com/optar/): **200 KB per A4 page**, Golay(23,12)\n669\t  — 3-of-12 bit redundancy. Needs 600 dpi print + 600 dpi scan.\n670\t- **PaperBak**: theoretical **500 KB per A4**, configurable Reed–Solomon. Windows-only and\n671\t  [reportedly unusable in practice due to alignment issues](https://blog.za3k.com/paper-archival).\n672\t- **QR codes for comparison: only ~70–100 KB per A4** — QR pays heavily for its finder\n673\t  patterns, quiet zones, and fixed RS.\n674\t\n675\tBoth chose *fixed-rate* codes because paper is a fixed-size medium — you know exactly how much\n676\tredundancy you can afford. **That is the opposite of screenferry's situation** (unbounded time\n677\tbudget, unknown loss rate), which is precisely why they chose RS/Golay and we should not.\n678\t\n679\t### 4.5 qrstream, QRFileTransfer, and the \"qr-filetransfer\" false friends\n680\t\n681\t**Important disambiguation:** most GitHub projects named `qr-filetransfer`\n682\t([svenkatreddy](https://github.com/svenkatreddy/qr-filetransfer),\n683\t[mattn](https://github.com/mattn/qr-filetransfer)) are **not optical transfer at all** — they\n684\trun a local HTTP server and put the *URL* in a QR code. The bytes go over WiFi. Not prior art.\n685\t\n686\tGenuine optical projects:\n687\t\n688\t- [xloem/qrstream](https://github.com/xloem/qrstream) — Android, splits data across successive\n689\t  QR codes. No fountain code.\n690\t- [LucaIaco/QRFileTransfer](https://github.com/LucaIaco/QRFileTransfer) — vanilla JS/HTML/CSS,\n691\t  camera-to-camera, closest existing thing to screenferry architecturally.\n692\t- [ganlvtech/qrcode-file-transfer](https://github.com/ganlvtech/qrcode-file-transfer) —\n693\t  screen + webcam.\n694\t- [mohankumarelec/airgapped-qr-code-transfer](https://github.com/mohankumarelec/airgapped-qr-code-transfer)\n695\t  — Vue + `pako` + `qrcode.js` + **`zbar-wasm`**. The `zbar-wasm` choice is a useful data\n696\t  point for screenferry's *decode* side (§7.5): it generally outperforms `jsQR` on blurry frames.\n697\t- [qifi-dev/qrs](https://github.com/qifi-dev/qrs) — 1 621 ★, the most polished, and the source\n698\t  of `luby-transform` (§3.2). **Closest existing project to screenferry.**\n699\t\n700\tNone publish throughput benchmarks; divan's remain the only rigorous numbers.\n701\t\n702\t### 4.6 Magic Wormhole / croc — why their chunking doesn't transfer\n703\t\n704\tBoth are network transports: a rendezvous server plus PAKE (SPAKE2) key agreement, with the\n705\tshort human code carrying only the *pairing secret*, never the data. They have a full\n706\tbidirectional TCP/WebSocket channel with retransmit, so their \"chunking\" is just streaming with\n707\tback-pressure — nothing to port.\n708\t\n709\t**What *is* worth stealing** is the human-factors idea: a short, memorable session code that\n710\tlets the receiver confirm it is talking to the right sender. screenferry's 32-bit `streamId` (§7.2)\n711\tcan be rendered as a 4-word or 6-character code on both screens so the user can visually confirm\n712\tthe pairing — valuable when two people are beaming files in the same room, where a stray QR from\n713\tsomeone else's screen could otherwise enter the camera's field of view.\n714\t\n715\t---\n716\t\n717\t## 5. Wire protocol and frame header design\n718\t\n719\t### 5.1 What each frame must carry\n720\t\n721\tEvery frame must be independently interpretable — the receiver may see its first frame at any\n722\tpoint. Required, in order of necessity:\n723\t\n724\t1. **Magic + version** — reject foreign QR codes (URLs, WiFi configs, other apps' frames)\n725\t   before they poison the decoder, and allow future format changes.\n726\t2. **Session ID** — bind frames to one transfer. Without it, a sender who restarts mid-stream\n727\t   silently corrupts the receiver's linear system. BC-UR's insight: **make this the payload's\n728\t   CRC-32**, so one field is session ID + PRNG seed + final integrity check.\n729\t3. **Total payload length** — to size the fragment array, compute `K`, and trim the final\n730\t   fragment's zero padding.\n731\t4. **Sequence number** — the fountain seed. With (2) it deterministically derives the index\n732\t   set, so **no index list is transmitted**.\n733\t5. **Compression flag** — the receiver must know whether to inflate.\n734\t6. **Per-frame integrity** — see §5.2.\n735\t\n736\tDeliberately **not** in the header:\n737\t\n738\t- **`K` / fragment count** — derivable as `K = ceil(payloadLen / fragLen)` where\n739\t  `fragLen = frameByteLength − HEADER_LEN` is directly observable, since every fountain symbol\n740\t  is exactly `fragLen` bytes. Saves 2 bytes/frame at the cost of one invariant: *`fragLen` must\n741\t  be constant for the lifetime of a stream* (no adaptive QR-version switching mid-transfer).\n742\t  BC-UR spends 1–2 bytes on explicit `seqLen`; we don't need to.\n743\t- **Filename / MIME / mtime** — these belong *inside* the payload (§5.4). Repeating a 40-byte\n744\t  filename in every frame would cost 3 % of airtime forever.\n745\t\n746\t### 5.2 Per-frame checksum: yes, 1 byte\n747\t\n748\tBBQr says \"QR error correction suffices\". For BBQr that is defensible; **for a fountain code it\n749\tis not.** With plain chunking, a corrupted frame damages one chunk and rescanning fixes it. With\n750\ta fountain code, a frame whose *header* is corrupted contributes a **wrong linear equation** to\n751\tthe system. GE still reaches rank K and still produces an answer — a wrong one — detected only\n752\tby the final CRC-32, at which point the entire multi-minute transfer must be discarded and\n753\trestarted with no diagnostic.\n754\t\n755\tQR's own Reed–Solomon usually reports failure rather than mis-correcting, but undetected\n756\tmis-correction is possible, especially at ECC level Low — which §4.1 says we want. A **1-byte\n757\tCRC-8 over the whole frame** catches 255/256 of corruptions for **0.08 %** of a 1 260-byte\n758\tframe. Cheap insurance against a catastrophic, undiagnosable failure. (Upgrade to CRC-16 if\n759\tfield testing shows mis-corrections; cost rises to 0.16 %.)\n760\t\n761\t### 5.3 Payload budget\n762\t\n763\tQR byte-mode capacities ([thonky.com](https://www.thonky.com/qr-code-tutorial/character-capacities)),\n764\twith screenferry's 13-byte header (§7.2) deducted, at the ECC-Low level §4.1 recommends:\n765\t\n766\t| Version | Modules | Byte cap (L) | Payload after header | Header cost |\n767\t|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|\n768\t| 15 | 77² | 520 | 507 | 2.5 % |\n769\t| 20 | 97² | 858 | 845 | 1.5 % |\n770\t| 25 | 117² | 1 273 | 1 260 | **1.0 %** |\n771\t| 30 | 137² | 1 732 | 1 719 | 0.8 % |\n772\t| 40 | 177² | 2 953 | 2 940 | 0.4 % |\n773\t\n774\tEstimated goodput, `p = 0.25`, fountain overhead 1.05:\n775\t\n776\t```\n777\tgoodput = fragLen × fps × (1 − p) / 1.05\n778\t```\n779\t\n780\t| Config | Goodput | 1 MB file |\n781\t|---|---:|---:|\n782\t| V20-L @ 12 fps | 7.2 KB/s | ~2 min 20 s |\n783\t| V25-L @ 8 fps | 7.2 KB/s | ~2 min 20 s |\n784\t| V30-L @ 8 fps | 9.8 KB/s | ~1 min 45 s |\n785\t| V40-L @ 6 fps | 12.6 KB/s | ~1 min 20 s |\n786\t\n787\tConsistent with divan's 1–9 KB/s (§4.1). **The honest expectation to set in the UI is\n788\t5–10 KB/s.** Higher QR versions look better on paper but decode worse on real cameras — V25–V30\n789\tis the sweet spot to start from, tuned empirically per §4.1's finding that fountain coding\n790\traises the optimal density.\n791\t\n792\t### 5.4 Payload container\n793\t\n794\tThe header stays minimal because metadata lives in the payload:\n795\t\n796\t```\n797\tcontainer := varint(metaLen) ‖ meta ‖ fileBytes\n798\tpayload   := compress(container)       // or container verbatim if compression didn't help\n799\tstreamId  := crc32(payload)\n800\t```\n801\t\n802\t`meta` is a small CBOR/JSON map: `{n: filename, t: mimeType, m: mtime}`. Compressing the\n803\tcontainer as a whole (rather than the file alone) means the filename compresses too, and there\n804\tis exactly one compression boundary to reason about.\n805\t\n806\t*Optional refinement:* the receiver cannot show the filename until the transfer completes. If\n807\tthat matters, interleave a **beacon frame** — same header, a distinct `magic_ver` low nibble —\n808\tcarrying plaintext metadata every ~30 frames, for ~3 % airtime. Recommended as a later\n809\tenhancement, not in v1.\n810\t\n811\t### 5.5 PRNG and index selection — must be bit-exact\n812\t\n813\tSender and receiver derive the same index set from `(streamId, seq)`. Any divergence\n814\t(floating-point, integer overflow, sign extension) silently corrupts the linear system.\n815\t\n816\t- Use **integer-only** PRNG arithmetic: `Math.imul` and `>>> 0` everywhere, never `Number`\n817\t  multiplication. `xoshiro128**` or `splitmix32` is sufficient; BC-UR's `SHA256(seqNum‖checksum)`\n818\t  → `Xoshiro256**` works but drags in a SHA implementation and BigInt for no benefit.\n819\t- Seed: `s = splitmix32(streamId ^ splitmix32(seq))`, then discard the first few outputs.\n820\t- Index selection: **partial Fisher–Yates** — `d` swaps against a sparse `Map` of displaced\n821\t  entries, O(d) time and memory. BC-UR's full `shuffle(indexes)` is O(K) allocation *per\n822\t  frame*; at K = 1000 and 10 fps that is 10 000 array elements/second of garbage for no reason.\n823\t- **Ship a cross-implementation test vector**: for a fixed `(streamId, seq, K)`, the expected\n824\t  index set. Cheap, and it catches the entire class of bit-exactness bugs.\n825\t\n826\t---\n827\t\n828\t## 6. Compression\n829\t\n830\t### 6.1 Availability\n831\t\n832\t`CompressionStream` / `DecompressionStream` are supported in all three engines\n833\t([web.dev](https://web.dev/blog/compressionstreams)): **Chrome/Edge 80, Firefox 113,\n834\tSafari 16.4**. Formats: `gzip`, `deflate`, `deflate-raw`.\n835\t\n836\tCaveat: **`deflate-raw` landed later than `gzip` in Chromium** (~103 vs 80); see\n837\t[caniuse](https://caniuse.com/mdn-api_compressionstream_compressionstream_deflate-raw). Feature-detect:\n838\t\n839\t```js\n840\tfunction pickFormat() {\n841\t  try { new CompressionStream('deflate-raw'); return 'deflate-raw'; }\n842\t  catch { return 'gzip'; }\n843\t}\n844\t```\n845\t\n846\t`deflate-raw` saves ~18 bytes of gzip header/trailer versus `gzip` — irrelevant for a whole-file\n847\tcompression, so `gzip` is a perfectly acceptable fallback. **Using the native API instead of\n848\t`pako` saves ~45 KB gzipped of bundle** — worth having on its own merits for a static app.\n849\t\n850\t### 6.2 When compression helps and when it hurts\n851\t\n852\tCompression happens **before** chunking, so it reduces `K` directly — and decode cost scales as\n853\t`K²` (§2.6), so a 2× compression ratio is a 2× airtime win *and* a 4× decode-cost win.\n854\t\n855\t| Content | Typical ratio | Verdict |\n856\t|---|---|---|\n857\t| Text, JSON, CSV, source code, logs | 0.15–0.35 | **Huge win** — 3–6× fewer frames |\n858\t| PSBT / CBOR / protobuf | 0.4–0.7 | Good win (BBQr measures 4–58 %) |\n859\t| Uncompressed BMP/WAV/TIFF | 0.3–0.6 | Good win |\n860\t| PDF (text-heavy) | 0.6–0.9 | Modest win |\n861\t| **JPEG, PNG, WebP, MP4, MP3, ZIP, gz, docx/xlsx** | **0.98–1.02** | **Skip** — deflate *expands* incompressible data by ~0.03 % plus 5-byte-per-32 KB stored-block overhead |\n862\t| Encrypted / random data | ~1.0 | **Skip** |\n863\t\n864\t### 6.3 Recommended policy\n865\t\n866\tCopy BBQr's runtime heuristic rather than sniffing file extensions (which lies — `.bin` could\n867\tbe anything, `.pdf` could be either):\n868\t\n869\t1. Compress the **first 128 KB** of the container with `deflate-raw`.\n870\t2. If `compressed / original > 0.92`, set `flags.comp = 0` and transmit verbatim.\n871\t3. Otherwise compress the whole container and set `flags.comp = 1`.\n872\t\n873\tThe sample step costs ~10 ms and is bounded regardless of file size. The 0.92 threshold leaves\n874\theadroom for files whose head is unrepresentative — being wrong costs a few percent of airtime,\n875\twhereas *always* compressing costs CPU and a tiny expansion on the very common case of sending\n876\ta photo.\n877\t\n878\t**Interaction with encryption:** if screenferry ever adds encryption, **compress first, then\n879\tencrypt.** Ciphertext is incompressible, so the reverse order silently disables compression.\n880\t(The CRIME/BREACH concern about compression-before-encryption does not apply — that attack\n881\tneeds an adaptive chosen-plaintext oracle, which a one-shot file transfer does not provide.)\n882\t\n883\t---\n884\t\n885\t## 7. Recommendations for screenferry\n886\t\n887\t### 7.1 Coding scheme — implement it ourselves, ~300 lines\n888\t\n889\t**Use a rateless XOR fountain code with BC-UR's framing conventions and a Gaussian-elimination\n890\tdecoder over GF(2).** Concretely:\n891\t\n892\t| Aspect | Decision | Why |\n893\t|---|---|---|\n894\t| Code family | LT-style random XOR fountain, **non-systematic** | Rateless is mandatory with no back-channel (§2.4); non-systematic beat systematic in every simulated cell (§4.2) |\n895\t| Degree distribution | **Harmonic, `Pr(d) ∝ 1/d`, capped at `d ≤ min(K, 64)`** | Best measured GE performance; the cap cuts encoder work ~10× at K = 1000 for +1.8 pp overhead (§2.6). Same family as BC-UR |\n896\t| Index selection | Derived from `(streamId, seq)` via `splitmix32` + partial Fisher–Yates | **Zero index bytes on the wire** — BC-UR's best idea (§4.2); `luby-transform` wastes 4 B/index (§3.2) |\n897\t| Decoder | **Full GF(2) Gaussian elimination, maintained in RREF incrementally** | 2–2.5× faster end-to-end than peeling at our K; overhead falls from +33…108 % to +2…7 % (§2.5) |\n898\t| Library | **None — write it** | Nothing available is both small and correctly decoded (§3.7) |\n899\t\n900\t**Expected performance:** ε ≈ **+2 % to +7 %** mean, **p99 ≈ +10 %** for K = 100–1000 — within\n901\ta few percent of RaptorQ, at ~3 KB of gzipped JS instead of 134 KB of WASM, with no patent\n902\tsurface.\n903\t\n904\t**Why not the alternatives:** RaptorQ is technically superior but costs 134 KB gzipped and a\n905\tQualcomm IPR footnote (§2.2) to save ~3 % overhead ≈ 15 frames on a typical transfer. Robust\n906\tsoliton is tuned for the decoder we are not using. Reed–Solomon is not rateless and a wrong\n907\trate guess is unrecoverable (§2.4). Online codes add a second layer for no measurable win at\n908\tour block sizes (§2.3).\n909\t\n910\t**Implementation sketch (~300 lines TS):**\n911\t\n912\t| Component | Lines |\n913\t|---|---:|\n914\t| `splitmix32` PRNG + partial Fisher–Yates index selection | ~40 |\n915\t| Harmonic degree sampler (cumulative table, binary search) | ~25 |\n916\t| CRC-32 (payload) + CRC-8 (frame) | ~35 |\n917\t| Encoder: slice, XOR-mix, emit infinite generator | ~50 |\n918\t| Decoder: incremental RREF over `Uint32Array` bitmasks + payload XOR | ~110 |\n919\t| Header pack/unpack + validation | ~40 |\n920\t\n921\tDecoder core:\n922\t\n923\t```\n924\trows: Map<pivotCol, {mask: Uint32Array, payload: Uint8Array}>\n925\t\n926\tonFrame(header, fragment):\n927\t  validate magic, version, CRC-8; if streamId differs from locked stream → ignore (or reset)\n928\t  K    = ceil(payloadLen / fragLen)\n929\t  idx  = deriveIndices(streamId, seq, K)     // no bytes on the wire\n930\t  mask = bitmask(idx);  data = fragment.slice()\n931\t  for each pivot p set in mask (ascending):\n932\t      if rows.has(p): mask ^= rows[p].mask;  data ^= rows[p].payload\n933\t  if mask is zero: return                    // linearly dependent, discard\n934\t  pivot = lowest set bit of mask\n935\t  reduce every existing row that has `pivot` set by (mask, data)   // keeps RREF\n936\t  rows.set(pivot, {mask, data})\n937\t  progress = rows.size / K                   // monotonic; unit rows reveal fragments early\n938\t  if rows.size === K:\n939\t      payload = concat(rows in pivot order).slice(0, payloadLen)\n940\t      if crc32(payload) === streamId: inflate → parse container → done\n941\t      else: header corruption slipped through — reset and warn\n942\t```\n943\t\n944\tMaintaining full RREF (rather than forward-elimination + a final back-substitution) costs ~2×\n945\tthe row operations but is still comfortably real-time (§2.6), needs no final pass, and yields\n946\tindividual fragments as soon as their row becomes a unit vector — which gives an honest,\n947\tmonotonically increasing progress bar.\n948\t\n949\t**Guard rails:**\n950\t\n951\t- `K < 8` → skip the fountain layer, cycle raw fragments (GE is pointless, and at K = 3 the\n952\t  coupon-collector penalty is negligible — this is BBQr's regime and BBQr is right about it).\n953\t- `K > 1500` → source-block partitioning via `flags.block` (§2.6); or raise the QR version first.\n954\t- Run the decoder in a **Web Worker**; camera decode and GE must not contend for the main thread.\n955\t- Ship the `(streamId, seq, K) → indices` test vector (§5.5).\n956\t\n957\t### 7.2 Proposed frame header — 13 bytes\n958\t\n959\tBinary QR byte-mode. All multi-byte fields big-endian.\n960\t\n961\t| Offset | Size | Field | Description |\n962\t|---:|---:|---|---|\n963\t| 0 | 1 | `magic_ver` | High nibble `0xB` = screenferry; low nibble = protocol version. **`0xB1`** = v1. Rejects foreign QR codes in one byte |\n964\t| 1 | 1 | `flags` | bits 0–1 `comp`: 0 = none, 1 = `deflate-raw`, 2 = `gzip`, 3 = reserved · bits 2–3 reserved (encryption, beacon) · bits 4–7 `block`: source-block index 0–15 |\n965\t| 2–5 | 4 | `streamId` | **CRC-32 of the encoded payload.** Triple duty: session discriminator, PRNG seed, whole-file integrity check |\n966\t| 6–8 | 3 | `payloadLen` | uint24 — encoded payload length in bytes (max 16 MiB). With observed `fragLen`, gives `K = ceil(payloadLen / fragLen)` |\n967\t| 9–11 | 3 | `seq` | uint24 — 1-based fountain sequence number (16.7 M frames ≈ 19 days at 10 fps). With `streamId`, seeds the index derivation |\n968\t| 12 | 1 | `fcrc` | CRC-8 over bytes 0–11 **and** the fragment. Prevents a mis-decoded frame from poisoning the linear system (§5.2) |\n969\t| 13 | `fragLen` | `fragment` | The XOR-mixed payload fragment. `fragLen = frameByteLength − 13`, constant for the stream |\n970\t\n971\t**Total overhead: 13 bytes/frame — 1.0 % at QR V25-L, 0.4 % at V40-L.**\n972\t\n973\tDerived, never transmitted: `K` (from `payloadLen` and `fragLen`), `fragLen` (from frame\n974\tlength), the fragment index set (from `streamId` + `seq`), and the number of source blocks.\n975\t\n976\tCompare: BC-UR spends ~10–15 bytes on CBOR-encoded `seqNum`/`seqLen`/`messageLen`/`checksum`\n977\t*plus* the Bytewords expansion; BBQr spends 8 ASCII chars but carries no session ID, no\n978\tchecksum, and no FEC; `luby-transform` spends `4×(degree+4)` ≈ 40+ bytes.\n979\t\n980\t**Two design rules this layout encodes:**\n981\t\n982\t- **Every field earns its bytes by doing more than one job.** `streamId` is session ID *and*\n983\t  PRNG seed *and* integrity check; frame length implies `fragLen` implies `K`. Anything that\n984\t  can be derived is derived.\n985\t- **Anything constant across the transfer belongs in the payload, not the header.** Filename,\n986\t  MIME type, and mtime go in the container (§5.4) — repeating them 500 times is pure waste.\n987\t\n988\t### 7.3 Compression\n989\t\n990\tNative `CompressionStream('deflate-raw')` with a `gzip` fallback (§6.1) — no `pako`, saving\n991\t~45 KB gzipped. Apply the 128 KB sample-and-threshold heuristic at 0.92 (§6.3), and record the\n992\toutcome in `flags.comp` so the receiver needs no heuristic of its own.\n993\t\n994\t### 7.4 Display parameters (starting point, to be tuned)\n995\t\n996\tFrom §4.1 and §5.3: **QR version 25–30, ECC level L, 8–12 fps.** Spend redundancy in the\n997\tfountain layer, not in the QR code's own Reed–Solomon — divan's data is unambiguous that ECC\n998\tLow wins because sparser QR codes decode faster and more reliably. Re-tune density *after* the\n999\tcodec works, since fountain coding raises the optimal chunk size (his optimum moved from\n1000\t550–900 B to 1 800–2 000 B).\n1001\t\n1002\t### 7.5 Receiver-side note\n1003\t\n1004\t[mohankumarelec/airgapped-qr-code-transfer](https://github.com/mohankumarelec/airgapped-qr-code-transfer)\n1005\tuses **`zbar-wasm`** rather than `jsQR`. Worth benchmarking both on blurry/low-light frames\n1006\tearly — at 10 fps the camera decode rate *is* the loss rate `p`, and every point of `p` costs\n1007\t`1/(1−p)` in airtime. Improving the decoder is likely the single highest-leverage optimisation\n1008\tavailable after the codec, and it is entirely independent of everything above.\n1009\t\n1010\t---\n1011\t\n1012\t## Architecture\n302\t\n303\t### 6.1 Layering\n304\t\n305\t**Modulation is swappable**, and **the block layer bounds everything below it**.\n306\t\n307\t```\n308\t┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐\n309\t│ UI          role select · progress · file in/out · coach │\n310\t├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤\n311\t│ Session     metadata · compression · resume · verify     │\n312\t├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤\n313\t│ Block       file ⇄ 192 KB blocks · scheduling · bitmap   │\n314\t├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤\n315\t│ Fountain    LT encode (endless) / GF(2) GE decode        │\n316\t│             K = 768 · matrix 72.0 KB · CONSTANT          │\n317\t├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤\n318\t│ Framing     13-byte header + payload → packet bytes      │\n319\t├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤\n320\t│ Modulation  ◄──────────────────────── SWAPPABLE ────────►│\n321\t│   Stage 1   tiled monochrome QR                          │\n322\t│   Stage 2   + RGB channel tripling                       │\n323\t│   Stage 3   libcimbar-derived grid codec                 │\n324\t├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤\n325\t│ Transport   canvas render loop  /  camera capture loop   │\n326\t└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘\n327\t```\n328\t\n329\t```ts\n330\tinterface Modulation {\n331\t  readonly packetsPerFrame: number;     // 1 plain, ~15 tiled, ~45 tripled\n332\t  readonly bytesPerPacket: number;      // = 13 + L\n333\t  encodeFrame(packets: Uint8Array[]): ImageData;\n334\t  decodeFrame(frame: VideoFrame): Uint8Array[];   // 0..n — never throws\n335\t}\n336\t```\n337\t\n338\t`decodeFrame` returning fewer packets than `packetsPerFrame` is the **normal case**.\n339\tNothing above this layer may care.\n340\t\n341\t### 6.2 Threads and ownership\n342\t\n343\tLayer boundaries and thread boundaries are **not** the same, which is worth stating\n344\texplicitly because it is a common source of bugs:\n345\t\n346\t| Component | Thread | Owns |\n347\t|---|---|---|\n348\t| UI, canvas paint | main | display |\n349\t| Frame encoder | worker | ring buffer (depth 3, I7) |\n350\t| QR decode pool | N workers | `VideoFrame` — MUST `close()` each or the pipeline stalls |\n351\t| GE decoder | 1 worker | the 72 KB matrix; single-owner, no sharing |\n352\t| OPFS writer | worker | `createSyncAccessHandle` is worker-only |\n353\t\n354\t**Backpressure policy:** if decode falls behind capture, camera frames are **dropped, not\n355\tqueued**. A queued frame is stale by the time it decodes, and queuing turns a throughput\n356\tproblem into a memory problem. Dropped frames are erasures, which the fountain code\n357\talready absorbs.\n358\t\n359\t### 6.3 Sender pipeline\n360\t\n361\t```\n362\tFile ──► [sample: compressible?] ──► CompressionStream ──► OPFS staging\n363\t  │            (D8, skip if not)                              │\n364\t  └──────────────── or straight through ─────────────────────┘\n365\t                                                              │\n366\t                                   cut into 192 KB blocks (D19)\n367\t                                                              │\n368\t                 ┌────────────────────────────────────────────┤\n369\t                 ▼                                            ▼\n370\t        beacon (D17/D21) every ~2 s          per block: slice → K=768 fragments\n371\t        filename · size · blockCount           → LT encode (d ≤ 64, D25)\n372\t        blockSize · L · K · hash · flags       → header → tile\n373\t                 │                                            │\n374\t                 └──────────────► frame mixer ◄───────────────┘\n375\t                                       │\n376\t                          ladder of 2–4 profiles (D16)\n377\t                                       │\n378\t                              DC-balance (D10) ──► canvas\n379\t                                       │\n380\t                     display at ≤ ½ measured camera fps (D9/D14)\n381\t```\n382\t\n383\tThe sender **dwells** on each block (§8.1), then advances, looping the file\n384\tcontinuously. It never terminates on its own — it cannot know when the receiver is done.\n385\t\n386\t> **Beacon clarification:** The beacon is a **packet** (distinguished by `PacketFlags.Beacon` in its header), not a separate frame. Sender-side throttling is detected when camera fps drops >30% while decode latency stays within +30%; in this case, the receiver MUST NOT duty-cycle. Invariants\n\nViolating one of these is a correctness bug, not a tuning choice. Each has an\nenforcement mechanism, because an invariant nothing checks is a comment.\n\n| # | Invariant | Enforced by |\n|---|---|---|\n| **I1** | Fragment length **L** MUST NOT change within a session (D15) | Session type makes `L` `readonly`; property test asserts a mid-session change throws |\n| **I2** | The degree distribution and the decoder MUST change together (D6); any distribution change MUST be simulated before merge | `sim/` assertions ported into the test suite; CI gate G4 |\n| **I3** | Fountain indices MUST be derived from `(streamId, blockIndex, seq)`, never transmitted (D7) | Golden test vector `(streamId, blockIndex, seq) → index set`, bit-exact across implementations |\n| **I4** | The file MUST NOT be fully materialised in memory on either side (D20) | Phase 1 flat-memory test over a synthetic 4 GB stream |\n| **I5** | **Exactly one payload block is GE-active at a time; the manifest stream has its own separate GE context** (bf-28b) | Session type permits two concurrent GE contexts: `active` for payload blocks and `manifestActive` for manifest blocks.
